newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian government group meets on human rights.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian government group meets on human rights.

text.p: A commission set up by Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha to investigate human rights abuses met for the first time on Monday amidst accusations of pro-government bias.

"People believe we will not be effective because the commission was set up by government so we are going to be stooges," Patrick Nwokedi, a retired supreme court judge and chairman of the National Human Rights Commission told Reuters in the capital Abuja.
"I assure people we will surprise them. We are going to carry out our work with the best of intentions," he added.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, has been shunned by western countries for repeated human rights violations.
Condemnation reached a peak in November after the hanging of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority activists for murder despite appeals for clemency from much of the world.
The human rights commission was set up by Abacha in June in response to a United Nations investigation into the execution of Saro-Wiwa, as well as the general human rights situation.
It is to make recommendations to government, but has no power to see that they are carried out.

"Many cases of human rights abuses in the country such as unlawful detention .. have been referred to the commission and are slated for hearing as soon as on-going arrangements are concluded," Nwokedi said.
He added that lack of funds had prevented the commission from starting work sooner.
Other members of the commission said that among the first cases being considered would be that of Campaign for Democracy chairman Beko Ransome-Kuti.
Ransome-Kuti is serving a fifteen year jail sentence for his part in an alleged plot to overthrow Abacha, for which former military head of state General Olusegun Obasanjo is also locked up.
Dozens of Nigerian opposition figures are in detention.
Most prominent among them is Moshood Abiola, who was arrested in 1994 for treason after declaring himself president on the basis of 1993 elections annulled by a former military government.
Last week two leading opposition members were released, while another was detained.
